summary:
Angola's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct took effect on 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era provision describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and, in the same instrument, made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation punishable by imprisonment. A continental survey published in October 2019 rated Angola as having gone furthest among African reforms of that period, both by removing the colonial offence and by attaching penalty to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services.

The constitutional layer is thinner than the statutory one. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights in Angola records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while the rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and expression are located across Title II of the same document. A visitor therefore has statutory protection against orientation-based discrimination without a constitutional guarantee expressly naming gender identity.

Angolan organisations submitted a shadow report on the country's compliance with the African Charter for the African Commission's 81st session in Banjul in October and November 2024, authored by Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA, Diversidade Masculina and others with ILGA and Synergia support, documenting human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. A separate submission by Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, ahead of the committee's 74th-session review of Angola, raises discrimination and health-access issues affecting lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people.

No specific law allows transgender people to change their gender marker on official documents or passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states that, in general, there should be no alteration of details entered into registration records, while section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status. Transgender people could possibly rely on section 87 to change their legal gender, but no worked procedure or precedent is recorded. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

No entry or visa provisions are recorded for Angola. The only entry-adjacent material available is external: an asylumlaw.org information packet on sexual minorities and HIV status used for asylum purposes, and UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office travel advice on local laws and customs.

Legally, people living with HIV/AIDS in Angola are entitled to health care services and to protection from employment discrimination. No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are recorded anywhere in the country. On relationship recognition, there is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant; in 2005 an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony was reported as 'shameless' and 'abominable' in national news magazines.
tangentialFactors:
Formal decriminalisation has not removed visible hostility. In April 2012 the BBC profiled kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, who became a mainstream star at 25, in a country the article described as Catholic and where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour. Trans visibility and criminalisation coexisted at that time, and the reporting indicates a social environment shaped by religious conservatism.

Political parties have not addressed LGBT issues: the three major political parties have not formally placed them in their platforms. In 2010 the Angolan Government refused to receive openly gay Isi Yanouka as the new Israeli ambassador, allegedly because of his sexual orientation; this was a diplomatic reception decision rather than a visa rule and does not establish an entry bar.

Comparatively, the October 2019 continental overview contrasted Angola's drafting strategy with that of Nigeria and Botswana, treating Angola as the jurisdiction that had gone furthest by combining decriminalisation with a discrimination offence.
localsOnly:
Two LGBT groups operate in Angola, and only one, the Iris Angola Association, has received official and legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018. At that time it had about 200 members, based in Luanda with offices in Benguela and Lubango. The government does allow non-governmental organisations to exist, and some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education.

Education-focused work for LGBTQ Angolans is nascent and underfunded. The first association, Acção Humana, launched in 2006 but has been unable to receive funding, and efforts to develop educational programmes specifically for LGBT people have struggled to obtain NGO funding. An HIV/AIDS educational programme for LGBT people is only beginning to develop through NGOs such as Population Services International, and a 2007 study estimated roughly five percent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not record whether any person has successfully used section 87 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 to alter a gender marker, so the practical availability of that route is not established here.

Unresolved: no entry, visa or border-screening provisions specific to trans visitors are sourced for Angola. The available material is limited to an asylum information packet and foreign-office travel advice, neither of which is an entry rule.

Not sourced: there are no youth- or minor-specific findings on travel, medication or education for Angola, and no recorded shelters, safe houses or gender-neutral facilities for LGBTQ people.
